read_by: builder agent, by hand against the excerpts
note: This is a reading done by hand against the excerpt `--show all` prints for each pair, before the model ever ran. The operator may overwrite any `human` label and re-run `--score`; the excerpt itself is not stored here, it is rebuilt from the manifest.

entries.sentence: A meta-analysis of 22 cross-sectional studies (21,677 participants, eight countries) reported shift work associated with higher odds of sleep disturbance (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.24–1.62), with rotating schedules (OR 1.48) and healthcare professionals (OR 1.56) showing the largest estimates; the cross-sectional design leaves the direction of the association uncertain [6].
entries.reason: Numbers, subgroup estimates and the cross-sectional caveat all match the excerpt.

entries.sentence: Life's Essential 8 lifestyle score was estimated to mediate about 39% of the cardiovascular association, a figure that depends on the modelling assumptions used [9].
entries.reason: 39.2% CVD mediation figure matches; the hedge about assumptions underclaims rather than overreaches.

entries.sentence: A separate large UK Biobank analysis reported a graded increase in atrial fibrillation risk across night shift categories (usual/permanent nights HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.02–1.32) and higher coronary heart disease risk with ≥10 years of night work (HR 1.37), which appeared unmodified by genetic predisposition [27].
entries.reason: Excerpt tests genetic modification only for AF, not for the CHD estimate the sentence also attaches it to.

entries.sentence: Among 143,410 female nurses followed 22–24 years, each five-year increment of rotating night shift work carried a type 2 diabetes hazard ratio of 1.31 (95% CI 1.19–1.44), with a significant additive interaction with unhealthy lifestyle [37].
entries.reason: N, follow-up, hazard ratio and interaction all match the excerpt exactly.

entries.sentence: UK Biobank cross-sectional data suggested higher diabetes odds with more night shifts per month (>8/month OR 1.36), though temporal ordering cannot be established from that design [48].
entries.reason: OR 1.36 for >8/month matches; the design/temporal hedge reflects the study's own cross-sectional scope.

entries.sentence: By contrast, an updated meta-analysis of 57 studies pooling several million participants found no association of ever night shift work with breast, prostate, ovarian, colorectal or stomach cancer [38].
entries.reason: All five named cancers are among the excerpt's null findings for ever exposure.

entries.sentence: A meta-analysis restricted to healthcare workers (12 studies, 12,132 breast cancer cases) found no excess for ever exposure (RR 1.05) and a modest excess at ≥20 years (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.01–1.55) [8].
entries.reason: 12 studies, 12,132 cases, RR 1.05 ever and RR 1.25 at ≥20 years match exactly.

entries.sentence: That longer-duration estimate lost significance in influence analysis and approached unity after correction for publication bias, and 60% of studies were rated high risk of bias for exposure assessment, so it may be fragile [8].
entries.reason: Loss of significance, approach to unity after correction, and the 60% high-RoB figure all appear.

entries.sentence: A meta-analysis of seven longitudinal studies reported shift work associated with adverse mental health outcomes (effect size 1.28, 95% CI 1.02–1.62) and depressive symptoms (1.33), with female shift workers apparently at higher odds of depressive symptoms (OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.39–2.14) [30].
entries.reason: Effect sizes 1.28/1.33 and the female OR 1.73 vs female non-shift workers match exactly.

entries.sentence: A consensus discussion paper by 15 shift work researchers judged the evidence sufficient to propose schedule limits — no more than three consecutive night shifts, shift intervals of at least 11 hours, and night shifts no longer than nine hours — while conceding that the underlying literature is limited [3].
entries.reason: 15 researchers, the three named limits, and the 'limited literature' caveat all match the excerpt.

entries.sentence: No randomised or controlled intervention appears to have tested whether changing shift schedules alters incidence of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or cancer; scheduling recommendations seem to rest largely on short-term physiological and observational evidence [3].
entries.reason: The excerpt never mentions RCTs at all; the sentence asserts their absence as if the source said so.

entries.sentence: How much of the excess risk might be modifiable through lifestyle rather than intrinsic to circadian misalignment has been estimated only by mediation and counterfactual modelling within a single cohort, and does not appear to have been tested prospectively [9].
entries.reason: Matches the paper's own mediation/counterfactual design and its call for further prospective study.
